blocks.title: What appears here, and what does not
text: A paper is published on this site only if RCF English created it, the copyright holder has given permission for it to be distributed, it has been personally approved for publication, or it can lawfully be **linked** from the official website that publishes it.

A paper is never published merely because a copy of it exists somewhere. This means the collection here grows more slowly than some others — deliberately. Read the [Copyright and Resource Policy](copyright-policy/).

blocks.heading: Choose your grade or literature section
intro: Every paper on this site sits in exactly one of the sections below, and choosing a section shows **all** of it — no title, province, term or subject has to be typed. Papers are listed newest year first, and any paper whose year is not printed on it appears under *Year not specified* rather than being left out.

blocks.title: What the “Clear scan” label means
text: Some papers carry a **Clear scan** label. It is given only after a person has opened the PDF and looked at the first page on screen, and seen that it is straight, sharp, complete, printed rather than handwritten, and carries **no student name**.

It is not awarded because the text copies out neatly. That test proved misleading: two Grade 10 papers read perfectly as text, yet one is visibly tilted and the other has *Teacher Copy* written across it by hand. Both are still in the collection, and neither carries the label.
Every other paper on the site is still worth using. It simply has not been through that check yet.

pages.title: How to Use Past Papers
pages.description: How to get real value from past papers: when to start, how to work under timed conditions, how to mark your own script, and the mistake almost every student makes.
pages.keywords: how to use past papers, timed practice, self marking, revision method

hero.text: Most students do past papers wrongly: too late, untimed, and without marking them. All three faults are easy to correct.

blocks.heading: The mistake almost everyone makes
text: Past papers are kept for the last month, worked through quickly, and never marked. The student finishes with a vague sense of having "done papers" and no idea what went wrong.
A past paper is not a test. It is a **teaching instrument**, and the teaching happens after you put the pen down.

blocks.heading: How to use one paper properly
intro: This takes about three hours in total for a full paper. Three papers used this way are worth more than fifteen worked through carelessly.

items.title: Work it under real conditions
text: By hand, to time, in one sitting, without notes and without your telephone. Anything else measures something other than what the examination measures.

items.title: Stop when the time stops
text: Draw a line where you were when the time ran out, then, if you wish, continue in a different colour. The line tells you the truth about your timing, which is information you badly need.

items.title: Leave it for a day
text: You cannot see your own errors an hour after writing. A day's gap makes you a much better marker of your own work.

items.title: Mark it yourself, with the guidance beside you
text: Use a marking scheme if one is lawfully available, or the checklists in the lessons on this site. Give yourself a mark, honestly. Being generous to yourself now is expensive later.

items.title: Write down your three biggest losses
text: Not every error — the three that cost the most marks. *Ran out of time on the essay. Wrote a notice without a date. Answered only half of question 4.*

items.title: Rewrite one answer properly
text: Only one. The weakest one. This single step is where nearly all the improvement happens, and it is the step almost everybody skips.

blocks.heading: When to start
text: **Earlier than you think.** Not in the last month — from the point at which you have covered a task type.
Learnt how a notice is laid out? Do the notice question from three papers this week. That is fifteen minutes' work and it makes the learning permanent.
Save complete, timed papers for the last two months. Use individual questions from the beginning.

blocks.heading: A term-by-term plan
columns: What to do with past papers
rows: Single questions on task types you have just studied. Untimed at first, then timed.
Half papers, timed. Mark them yourself. Begin keeping a list of your recurring errors.
One complete paper a fortnight, under full conditions. Mark, note three losses, rewrite one answer.
One complete paper a week. Revise your own marked scripts, not new material.
No new papers. Reread your own error list and your best answers. Sleep.

blocks.heading: Marking your own script honestly
text: Self-marking is a skill, and it can be learnt. Ask these questions of each answer in turn.
bullets: **Did I answer the question that was asked**, or one close to it?
**Did I answer every part** of a multi-part question?
**Is the form correct** — notice, email, letter, essay, speech?
**Is the length appropriate** to the marks?
**Would someone else understand my handwriting** here?
**How many marks did I lose to errors I could have caught** in the last ten minutes?
**Where exactly did I run out of time?** — this is usually the largest single loss on the paper.

blocks.title: About model answers
text: When you compare your answer with a model, you are not looking for the same words. You are looking for the same **structure**.

Model answers on this site are teaching material written by RCF English. They are not official answers and they are not the only acceptable ones. Do not memorise them — a memorised answer will not fit the question you are actually asked.

pages.title: O/L English Past Papers

pages.keywords: O/L English past papers, Ordinary Level English papers, model papers, Grade 11

hero.text: Papers for the Ordinary Level English Language examination. Study the task before you attempt the paper — the lessons are linked below.

blocks.heading: What these papers are
text: Every paper here is for the Ordinary Level English Language examination or for the grades that lead to it, arranged by grade with the newest year first. Grade 11 holds the O/L papers themselves, because the examination is sat at the end of Grade 11; the lower grades hold school and zonal papers that use the same question types at an easier level.
They are linked from where they are published, not copied onto this site. If a link ever fails, please [tell us](corrections/) and it will be checked.

blocks.heading: How to use a past paper properly
text: Most students use past papers too early and too fast. A paper is a measuring instrument, and measuring is useless before there is something to measure.
bullets: **Learn the task before you attempt it.** Read the [Paper I guide](ol-english/paper-i/) and the [Paper II guide](ol-english/paper-ii/) first, so you know what each section is asking for. A student who does not know what a task wants cannot practise it.
**Do one section at a time, untimed, at the start.** Accuracy first. Speed is a separate skill and comes later.
**Then do whole papers under time,** in one sitting, with no dictionary and no phone. This is the only way to find out what happens to your handwriting and your planning in the last twenty minutes.
**Mark it against the [marking schemes](past-papers/marking-schemes/), not against your feelings.** A paper you marked generously has taught you nothing.
**Write down what you lost marks for, not the score.** Three sittings later, check whether the same three things are still costing you marks. That list is your revision plan.

blocks.heading: The mistake to avoid
text: Reading a paper and its answers together, without attempting it, feels productive and is nearly worthless. The learning is in the attempt: the moment when you do not know what to write is the moment that teaches you something. Keep the answers closed until your own attempt is finished, however uncomfortable that is.

pages.title: O/L Literature Past Papers
pages.description: Every O/L English Literature paper on the site, for Grades 10 and 11 and for the examination itself, listed newest year first.
pages.keywords: O/L Literature past papers, English Literature papers, context questions, essay questions

hero.text: Papers for O/L English Literature. Remember that a Literature paper depends on the prescribed texts of its year — check which texts a paper was set on before using it.

blocks.heading: What these papers are, and one thing to check first
text: These are O/L English Literature papers, arranged by grade with the newest first. Unlike a language paper, a Literature paper can only be answered by somebody who has studied the particular texts it asks about.

**So check the texts before you use an older paper.** Prescribed texts change from time to time. A paper on a poem or play you are not studying is still useful for practising *how* to answer, but you cannot practise the content. The [prescribed texts page](ol-literature/texts/) lists what is set now.

blocks.heading: How to use a Literature paper
text: A Literature answer is marked on what you notice in the text and how well you argue it, not on how much you remember about the author.
bullets: **Plan before you write.** Three or four lines: your argument, and the two or three moments in the text that prove it. Answers that begin without a plan retell the story, and retelling earns very little.

**Answer the question that was asked.** The commonest loss of marks in Literature is a good essay about the wrong thing. Underline the words in the question that limit it, and check them again when you finish.
**Quote short and quote from memory.** One well-chosen phrase, used to make a point, is worth more than four lines copied out. Practise with the book closed, because in the examination it will be.

**Practise the context questions separately** from the essays: they reward precision rather than length. See [context questions](ol-literature/context-questions/) and [essay questions](ol-literature/essay-questions/).
**Time the questions against their marks.** Running out of time on the last question is a planning failure, not a knowledge failure, and it is the easiest kind to fix.

blocks.title: Prescribed texts change between years
text: A past Literature paper may be set on texts that are no longer prescribed. The **questions** remain useful — they show you the kinds of question asked and how they are worded — even when the texts differ. Check the current official syllabus for your own year.

hero.text: Papers for Advanced Level English Literature. Unseen appreciation questions from any year are useful, whatever the prescribed texts were.

blocks.heading: What these papers are, and which years still apply
text: These are A/L English Literature papers, newest first. Two things are worth knowing before you download one.

**Papers from earlier years may test texts that are no longer prescribed.** The set texts have changed over the years, so an older paper can ask about a novel or play nobody now studies. Such a paper is still useful for practising the *form* of an answer - the wording of the questions, the balance between argument and evidence - but not for revising content. Check the [prescribed texts page](al-literature/prescribed-texts/) for what is set now.

**Some official marking material is marked confidential and is not reproduced here.** Where that is the case the paper is linked without it, and the [answer development](al-literature/answer-development/) pages explain what a strong answer contains instead.

blocks.heading: How to work with an A/L Literature paper
text: At this level the examiner is looking for an argument that could only have been written by somebody who had read the text closely and thought about it.
bullets: **Read the whole paper before choosing.** The question that looks easiest at first glance is often the one with the least to say about it.
**Spend the first five minutes planning, not writing.** An A/L essay lives or dies on its structure: a position, three developed points, and a conclusion that does more than repeat the introduction.
**Build your own quotation bank** as you study - eight to ten short quotations for each text, each attached to an idea rather than to a plot event.
**Write at least three full essays under time before the examination.** Writing a complete essay in the time allowed is a physical skill as much as an intellectual one.

**Compare your answer with the [critical appreciation](al-literature/critical-appreciation/) and [essay question](al-literature/essay-questions/) guidance** rather than with a memorised model. Examiners recognise a memorised essay immediately.

blocks.title: Old papers are still useful — for two things
bullets: **Unseen appreciation questions never expire.** A poem or passage set ten years ago is exactly as useful for practice as one set last year, because nothing was prescribed.

**Question wording is stable even when texts change.** Reading twenty essay questions on texts you have not studied teaches you how such questions are constructed — which is precisely what you need in order to read your own question properly.

pages.title: Model Papers
pages.description: Model papers written in the style of the examination for O/L English, O/L Literature and A/L Literature, for timed practice.
pages.keywords: model papers, practice papers, mock papers, English, Literature

hero.text: Papers written in the style of the examination. Useful when you have exhausted the real papers, or want practice on a specific format.

blocks.heading: What a model paper is - and what it is not
text: A model paper is written by a teacher, a publisher or a school to resemble the real examination. It is not set by the Department of Examinations, and no model paper can promise to predict what will be asked.

That makes model papers useful for one thing in particular: **volume**. There are only so many real past papers, and a student who needs twenty attempts at a task type will run out of them. Model papers fill that gap.

blocks.heading: How to use them without being misled
text: The danger of model papers is calibration. Some are noticeably harder than the real examination and some noticeably easier, so a mark from a model paper is not a reliable measure of where you stand.
bullets: **Practise on model papers; measure on real past papers.** Keep two or three genuine papers unopened until the last few weeks, and use those to judge your readiness.

**Treat an odd question as an opportunity, not an error.** If a model paper asks something in an unfamiliar way, that is useful: the real examination will also phrase something in a way you did not expect.
**Check the syllabus, not the year.** A model paper written for an earlier syllabus may test content that has since moved or gone.
**Mark to the real standard.** Use the official [marking schemes](past-papers/marking-schemes/) for the closest real paper rather than the model paper's own answers, which are often more generous.

blocks.title: What a model paper is
text: A model paper is written to resemble the examination in structure, in the kinds of question asked and in the time it takes. It is **not** an official paper and is not set by any examination authority.
Model papers published here are written by RCF English, or are published with the permission of whoever wrote them. The source is shown against each one.

pages.title: School Term-Test Papers
pages.description: First, second and third term test papers in English and Literature set by schools, where they may lawfully be published or linked.
pages.keywords: term test papers, school papers, first term, second term, third term

hero.text: Term-test papers are shorter than the examination and are often better graded for practice during the year.

blocks.heading: What term test papers are good for
text: These are the papers schools and zones set for the first, second and third terms. They differ from examination papers in one way that makes them valuable: **a term test only covers what has been taught by that point in the year.**

That makes them the right practice for the middle of a school year, when a full examination paper would mostly ask about material a class has not reached yet - which discourages students for no good reason.

blocks.heading: How to use them
text: Expect variation. Different schools and zones write to different levels of difficulty and set out their papers differently, and that variation is itself worth meeting before the real examination.
bullets: **Match the term, not just the grade.** A third-term paper used in the first term will look impossible; the same paper in November is a fair test.
**Use them to find gaps early.** A term test that exposes a weakness in September can still be fixed. The same weakness found in a past paper in December cannot.
**Do not compare marks between schools.** Two papers marked in two schools are not the same measurement. Compare your own performance across two papers from the same source instead.
**Keep the papers your own school sets.** Your teachers' papers tell you how your teachers ask questions, which no downloaded paper can.

blocks.heading: Term-test papers
intro: Choose a grade or literature section to see every first, second and third term paper for it.

blocks.title: A note on school papers
text: A term-test paper belongs to the school or the teacher who set it. RCF English publishes such a paper only with permission, or links to it where a school has published it itself.
**Teachers:** if you would like your school's papers made available here, [get in touch](contact/). Please confirm that you are entitled to give that permission.

pages.title: Provincial Papers
pages.description: English and Literature papers set at provincial level, where they may lawfully be published or linked from an official source.
pages.keywords: provincial papers, provincial examination, English papers

hero.text: Provincial papers are usually closer to the national examination in style and standard than school papers, which makes them valuable practice.

blocks.heading: Why provincial papers are worth using
text: These papers are set by provincial departments of education. They follow the same national syllabus as the examination, but they are written by different people - and that is exactly what makes them useful.

A student who has only ever practised on papers from one source learns that source's habits: its favourite question types, its phrasing, the order it puts things in. The examination will not share those habits. Meeting the same content asked differently, several times, is what makes a student steady on the day.

blocks.heading: How to use them
text: Papers from a province other than your own are not harder or easier in any systematic way; they are simply written by another hand.
bullets: **Use them for unfamiliar phrasing.** When a question you know the answer to is worded in a way you have not seen, that discomfort is the practice. Note the wording rather than the answer.
**Work across provinces deliberately** in the last two months, one paper from each, rather than three from the same province.
**Check the year against your syllabus** before using an older provincial paper, as with any paper on this site.
**Mark against the official [marking schemes](past-papers/marking-schemes/) where one exists** for the equivalent national paper, so your standard does not drift.

pages.title: Revision Papers
pages.description: Shorter revision papers focused on a single skill or section — grammar, comprehension, writing tasks, context questions — for practice during the year.
pages.keywords: revision papers, practice papers, skill practice, short papers

hero.text: A full paper takes three hours and a whole afternoon to use properly. A revision paper takes thirty minutes, which means you will actually do it.

blocks.heading: What revision papers are
text: Revision papers are shorter and more focused than full examination papers. They are meant for the weeks when there is no longer time to sit a complete paper every day, but there is still time to repair particular weaknesses.

A full paper takes a long sitting and a long marking session. A revision paper takes a fraction of that, which means it can actually be done - and a short paper that gets done beats a long one that does not.

blocks.heading: Where they fit in the last weeks
text: The last month before an examination is not the time to meet new material. It is the time to make what you already know reliable under pressure.
bullets: **Use one every second day, marked the same day.** Practice you have not marked is only writing.
**Alternate the skill.** Reading one day, writing the next, so that no single weakness swallows the whole week.
**Keep two full past papers for the final fortnight,** done in one sitting at the real length, so the examination is not the first long paper you have written in a month.
**Stop adding new material in the last ten days** and use revision papers only to rehearse what is already there. Anxiety in the final week comes mostly from trying to learn something new too late.

blocks.title: Why short papers are often more useful
text: A complete paper is the right instrument in the last two months. Before that it is usually the wrong one: it takes too long, it mixes too many skills together, and the feedback arrives too late to be acted on.
A revision paper on one task — notices, or context questions, or tenses — can be attempted, marked and learnt from in under an hour. Six of those in a term will teach more than two complete papers.

pages.title: Question Banks
pages.description: Collections of questions grouped by task and topic rather than by paper — notices, emails, letters, essays, context questions and more.
pages.keywords: question bank, practice questions, task questions, topic questions

hero.text: When you have just learnt how a task works, you do not want a whole paper. You want ten questions on that one task.

blocks.heading: What a question bank is for
text: A question bank is not a paper. It is a set of questions of the **same kind**, collected together, so that a student can practise one thing repeatedly instead of meeting it once every few weeks.
That is the difference that matters. A whole paper gives one attempt at each task type; a question bank gives ten attempts at the one task type that is costing you marks.

blocks.heading: How to use a question bank
text: Use it to repair a specific weakness that you have already identified from a marked paper. Working through a bank at random is much less useful than working through the one your own errors point at.
bullets: **Find the weakness first.** Mark two past papers, list what you lost marks for, and choose the bank that matches the top item on the list.

**Do ten in a row, then stop and look for the pattern.** Ten answers of the same type make an error visible that one answer hides - always mishearing the same word, always forgetting the same tense, always writing past the word limit.
**Say the rule out loud before the next ten.** Learners who can state what they were getting wrong fix it; learners who just do more questions usually repeat it.
**Come back a week later, not the next day.** Practising the same task type twice in one sitting flatters your memory. A week's gap tests whether you actually learnt it.

hero.text: A marking scheme is the most useful document in revision — and the most misused.

blocks.title: Marking schemes and copyright
text: An official marking scheme belongs to the body that produced it. RCF English publishes one only where the copyright holder has given permission, and otherwise links to the official source where the official source publishes it.
Marking **guidance** written by RCF English is original material and is published freely. It is clearly distinguished from any official scheme.

blocks.heading: Marking schemes and guidance
blocks.sectionNote: Every marking scheme on the site that may lawfully be published or linked, newest year first. The grade and subject are printed on each card.

blocks.heading: How to use a marking scheme
numbered: **Write the answer first.** A marking scheme read before the attempt teaches nothing, because you cannot then see what you would have done.
**Mark against it honestly.** Being generous to yourself is the commonest self-marking error and the most expensive.

**Look at what it rewards, not only at the answers.** A scheme tells you what examiners are looking for — content points, structure, accuracy, appropriateness — and that information transfers to every other question.
**Do not memorise scheme answers.** They are answers to that question, not templates.
**Notice where marks are cheap.** Most schemes contain marks for things like correct form and complete answers, which cost nothing but attention.

pages.title: Model Answers
pages.description: Model answers for past and model papers, written by RCF English, with notes explaining how each answer is built and why it works.
pages.keywords: model answers, sample answers, worked answers, past papers

hero.text: Answers to compare your own against — for structure, not for wording.

blocks.heading: What a model answer is for
text: A model answer shows what a full answer to a question looks like: how it is organised, how much detail it gives, and where it puts the point it is making. It is a demonstration, not something to be learnt by heart.

Used well, one model answer can change how a student writes every answer afterwards. Used badly - memorised and reproduced - it costs marks, because examiners recognise a memorised answer at once and because the question in front of you is never quite the question it answered.

blocks.heading: How to use one
text: The order matters more than anything else on this page: **attempt, then compare.** A model answer read before your own attempt replaces your thinking instead of improving it.
bullets: **Write your own answer first,** even a poor one, even an incomplete one. The gaps in your attempt are what the model is going to explain.
**Then compare structure, not wording.** Where does the model make its point? What does it do with evidence? How long is the introduction really? Those are transferable; its sentences are not.
**Mark the difference in one line.** *Mine retold the story; the model argued a point.* That line is worth more than rewriting the model out.
**Answer the same question again a week later,** without looking at either. What survives is what you learnt.
**Never learn an answer by heart for an essay question.** Learn the shape, the evidence and the argument, and write it fresh.

blocks.title: What these are, and are not
bullets: Model answers on this site are **written by RCF English** as teaching material.
They are **not official answers**, and they are not the only acceptable answers.
**Do not memorise them.** A memorised answer does not fit the question you are actually asked, and examiners recognise it.
Read the notes under each answer. The notes are the lesson; the answer is the example.
